The passage explicitly links reduced measurement variability to the simplified freeze-boil extraction and optimization of lysis cycles, not to the detection chemistry. Therefore, this option is not the most direct way to address sample-processing measurement error.

24.Option: The enhanced secretion of IFN-γ and TNF-α by T cells in CCR8-KO mice compared to WT mice demonstrates that the host immune response is a primary driver of disease severity in the absence of CCR8 signaling
Evidence: Flow cytometric analysis revealed that CCR8-deficient T cells exhibited a stronger anti-parasitic immune response capacity. At multiple time points post-infection, the proportions of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in the livers of infected KO mice secreting IFN-γ and TNF-α were significantly higher than in the infected WT group (Fig 6A).
In vivo ultrasonographic assessment showed that at 12 wpi, the size of parasitic lesions in the livers of infected KO mice was significantly smaller than in the infected WT group (Fig 5A-B).
This result strongly suggests that the absence of CCR8 signaling effectively controlled parasite growth and infiltration, thereby reducing the burden of space-occupying lesions in the liver.
24.Rationale: These quoted passages show that enhanced IFN-γ and TNF-α secretion in CCR8-KO mice is associated with improved parasite control and reduced lesion size. That evidence supports the idea that a stronger effector immune response reduces disease severity (i.e., immunity is protective), not that the host immune response is the primary driver of severity. Therefore this finding does not support the claim that the host immune response itself exacerbates disease severity; it indicates the opposite (that restored effector responses alleviate disease).

24.Option: The persistent elevation of CCR8+ Tregs in infected mice beyond normal physiological decline indicates active immune dysregulation that exacerbates disease severity
Evidence: multiple studies have confirmed significant enrichment of Tregs in the local lesions of AE patients and infected animal models, correlating with disease progression [7, 8, 11].

Immunofluorescence co-localization, we observed FOXP3 and CCR8 co-expressed on infiltrating lymphocytes surrounding the liver lesions, with clear co-localization signals visible under high-magnification fields (Fig 2D).

Of critical importance, at 24 weeks, when the frequencies in controls had declined, they remained persistently high in the infected group (e.g., CD4 ⁺ CCR8 ⁺ : 6.40 ± 1.19% vs. 3.49 ± 0.86%, P < 0.01), indicating that the infection not only amplified a physiological wave but also abrogated its normal resolution.
The CCR8/CCL1 axis is a key driver in the formation of the immunosuppressive microenvironment in the AE liver.
24.Rationale: These quotes document (1) enrichment of Tregs correlating with disease progression, (2) co-localization of FOXP3 (a Treg marker) with CCR8 at lesion sites, and (3) that CCR8+ Treg frequencies remain abnormally elevated in infected mice when controls decline. Together this supports active, infection-driven immune dysregulation (Treg-mediated immunosuppression) that would promote parasite survival and disease progression rather than merely reflecting parasite burden.

24.Option: The expansion of CCR8+ T cells in infected mice at 2 and 24 wpi, despite declining levels in controls, suggests that the immune system is actively suppressing parasite clearance and worsening disease severity
Evidence: the subset expressing CCR8 (CD4+ CCR8+ Tregs) showed significant expansion both in the early (2 wpi) and late (24 wpi) stages of infection (Fig 3A).

At both 12 and 24 weeks, the proportions of all CCR8 ⁺ T cell subsets (CD3 ⁺ , CD4 ⁺ , CD8⁺) in infected mice were significantly elevated compared to their time-matched controls (e.g., CD4 ⁺ CCR8⁺ at 12 weeks: 56.10 ± 8.80% vs 33.37 ± 6.98%, P < 0.01).

Of critical importance, at 24 weeks, when the frequencies in controls had declined, they remained persistently high in the infected group ... indicating that the infection not only amplified a physiological wave but also abrogated its normal resolution.
this numerically expanded CCR8+ T cell population exhibited a markedly suppressed functional state.

CCR8-positive CD4+ and CCR8-positive CD8+ T cells generally had a significantly reduced capacity to secrete key cytotoxic mediators (like perforin) and pro-inflammatory cytokines (including IFN-γ, TNF-α, and IL-2)
24.Rationale: The passages show both expansion of CCR8+ T cells at early and late time points and that these CCR8+ cells are functionally suppressed (reduced effector cytokine and cytotoxic mediator production). The combination of increased numbers of functionally impaired CCR8+ cells supports the interpretation that infection-driven immune alterations actively impede parasite clearance (via immunosuppression) and thereby contribute to disease severity rather than merely reflecting parasite load.

24.Option: The significant increase in liver weight and liver-to-body weight ratio in infected WT mice compared to controls indicates that immune-mediated inflammation directly causes tissue damage and disease severity
Evidence: Compared to the uninfected control (CON) group, the absolute liver weight of infected wild-type (WT) mice was significantly increased at 12 and 24 weeks post-infection (Fig 1A).

The liver-to-body weight ratio, calculated to account for body weight effects, was significantly higher than the control group at all time points post-infection (2, 12, 24 wpi) (Fig 1B), indicating substantial hepatomegaly.
Given that parasitic lesions are the primary cause of hepatomegaly in infected mice, we used liver weight measurements to assess the overall parasite load and pathological damage indirectly.
24.Rationale: While liver enlargement and higher liver-to-body weight ratio indicate greater disease burden, the authors explicitly state that these measures primarily reflect parasite lesion burden (space-occupying parasitic lesions). Thus increased liver weight is not specific evidence that host immune-mediated inflammation is the direct cause of tissue damage; it can largely reflect parasite load. Therefore this finding does not strongly support that the host immune response, rather than parasite burden, drives disease severity.

24.Option: The upregulation of CCL1 and FOXP3 mRNA in infected WT mice at 24 wpi indicates that the host immune response actively promotes parasite survival and disease progression through immunosuppression
Evidence: Immunohistochemical staining showed that in the late stage of infection (24 wpi), the percentage area positive for the chemokine receptor CCR8, its ligand CCL1, and the Treg key transcription factor FOXP3 was significantly higher in the liver tissues of infected WT mice compared to the uninfected control group (Fig 2A-B).

At the gene transcription level, quantitative real-time PCR results confirmed that the relative mRNA expression of CCR8, CCL1, and FOXP3 in the liver was significantly upregulated at 24 wpi; analysis of earlier time points indicated that this upregulation was time-dependent and most prominent in the late stage of infection (Fig 2C).

Immunofluorescence co-localization, we observed FOXP3 and CCR8 co-expressed on infiltrating lymphocytes surrounding the liver lesions, with clear co-localization signals visible under high-magnification fields (Fig 2D).

both immunohistochemical and qRT-PCR analyses confirmed that the expression levels of CCL1 and FOXP3 in the livers of infected KO mice were significantly lower than in the infected WT group (Fig 5E-G).
These phenotypic data clearly demonstrate that the absence of CCR8 signaling effectively curtails the liver pathological damage induced by E. m infection.
24.Rationale: Upregulation of CCL1 (the CCR8 ligand) together with FOXP3 (a Treg marker) at the late stage, plus co-localization of CCR8 and FOXP3 at lesions, provides direct molecular and spatial evidence that the host mounts an immunosuppressive response that is orchestrated at the lesion site. The fact that CCR8 deficiency reduces CCL1/FOXP3 expression and ameliorates pathology links this immunosuppressive response causally to worse disease. Therefore these findings strongly support that host immune modulation (immunosuppression) actively promotes parasite survival and disease progression, not merely mirrors parasite burden.

25.Option: The high viral load in the blood of infants under 3 months, coupled with the absence of severe neurological outcomes, suggests that systemic viremia alone is insufficient to cause neurological damage
Evidence: blood VL varied significantly across age groups, with infants younger than 3 months presenting with the highest VL (p < 0.0001).

We found no clear relationship between blood VL and the clinical presentation of children, similar to the findings from an Indian study [26]. This suggests that the blood viral load may not contribute significantly to the severity of CHIKV infection.
children aged over one year accounted for up to 75% of severe cases, whereas they represented only 32.6% of the cohort.
25.Rationale: The passage reports that infants <3 months had the highest blood viral loads yet the distribution of severe neurological cases was concentrated in older children (75% of severe cases were >1 year). The authors explicitly state there was no clear relationship between blood VL and clinical presentation and that blood VL "may not contribute significantly to the severity". Together, these observations support the inference that high systemic viremia alone does not explain the neurological outcomes.

25.Option: The lack of intrathecal antibody response in the CSF, despite detectable viral RNA, suggests that the virus does not replicate within the central nervous system
Evidence: This hypothesis should have been further explored by assessing cytokines and intrathecal antibody response, but this could not be done given the small quantity of CSF available and the retrospective study design.
25.Rationale: The passage does not report a measured absence of intrathecal antibody response; rather it states that assessment of intrathecal antibody response could not be performed due to limited CSF volume. Because the study did not measure intrathecal antibodies, one cannot cite a lack of intrathecal antibody response from this dataset as evidence that CNS replication is absent.

25.Option: The absence of pleocytosis in the CSF, despite high viral load, suggests that the virus does not replicate within the central nervous system
Evidence: Pleiocytosis (white cells ≥ 5/mL) was observed in 5 cases but never exceeded 10 white cells/mL.
All CSF samples were CHIKV positive by RT-PCR, except in two children.

Since the time between lumbar puncture and blood sampling was ≤ 24h, and hemorrhagic CSF samples were excluded from calculation, these findings suggest that there might be passive diffusion of viral RNA from the blood to the CSF, rather than intrathecal replication.
25.Rationale: The study found detectable CHIKV RNA in CSF but very little pleocytosis (minimal inflammatory cells), and the authors interpret the pattern (high blood VL, lower CSF VL, minimal CSF inflammation) as compatible with passive diffusion of viral RNA rather than active intrathecal replication. Thus the absence of pleocytosis alongside CSF RNA supports the conclusion that CNS replication is unlikely to be the main driver of neurological outcomes.

25.Option: The absence of a correlation between CSF viral load and neurological severity, despite consistent CSF viral presence, suggests that intrathecal viral replication is not the primary driver of neurological outcomes
Evidence: No relation was found between the severity of neurological manifestations and the VL in the blood or CSF (Table 3).

By multivariable analysis, CSF viral load was not significantly associated with the severity of neurological manifestations (OR = 1.03 [95% CI 0.62, 1.85]) after adjustment for age and time between onset of clinical signs and lumbar puncture.
All CSF samples were CHIKV positive by RT-PCR, except in two children.
25.Rationale: The key direct evidence in the passage is that CSF viral load did not correlate with neurological severity (multivariable OR ~1.03, not significant), even though CSF was frequently RT-PCR positive. That lack of association is the strongest direct indication reported that the magnitude of virus in the CNS is not the primary determinant of neurological outcome.

26.Option: The presence of L. infantum in a N. squamipes individual, confirmed by xenodiagnosis and PCR, demonstrates that this species can serve as a competent host in the transmission cycle despite low parasitemia
Evidence: Detection of L. infantum in three small mammals (11.76%), one D. albiventris and two N. squamipes, suggests that these species may serve as alternative hosts, despite the traditional role of domestic dogs as the principal urban reservoirs of VL.
Leishmania infections were identified exclusively through xenodiagnoses, likely due to low parasitemia.
ID09 (N. squamipes) was co-infected with L. infantum, detected through xenodiagnoses followed by PCR of fed sand flies, and T. lainsoni, isolated from blood culture.
26.Rationale: While detection of L. infantum in N. squamipes (including xenodiagnosis and PCR from fed sand flies) provides evidence that this species can harbor Leishmania and potentially infect vectors, the passage emphasizes that Leishmania infections were identified "exclusively through xenodiagnoses, likely due to low parasitemia." Xenodiagnoses alone is a proxy and, given low parasitemia and lack of parasite isolation from host tissues in many cases, this finding is weaker evidence for sustained transmission cycles than host infections confirmed by multiple direct diagnostic methods (culture, PCR, sequencing). Therefore this option does not most strongly support sustained transmission cycles compared with the stronger evidence provided by multi-method confirmation of infection.

26.Option: The detection of T. cruzi in a D. albiventris individual through multiple diagnostic methods, including blood culture and PCR, indicates that this species is a competent reservoir for sustained transmission cycles
Evidence: Trypanosoma cruzi infection (DTU TcI confirmed by molecular analysis) was detected in two D. albiventris individuals.

Microscopic observation of flagellates in triatomines following xenodiagnoses suggests host infectiousness for Trypanosoma sp., while species identification was confirmed by PCR and sequencing of the parasites isolated from blood or tissues.

Among the positive mammals, only one individual (D. albiventris, ID16) tested positive for the same parasite (T. cruzi) by all diagnostic approaches (culture and direct PCR, both confirmed by 18S rRNA sequencing).
26.Rationale: This option presents the strongest support from the study for potential sustained transmission cycles because the D. albiventris individual (ID16) tested positive by multiple complementary and direct diagnostic methods (culture, PCR, and sequencing), and microscopy of triatomines post-xenodiagnoses suggested host infectiousness. Multi-method confirmation indicates viable infection and capacity to infect vector bugs, which are key criteria for reservoir competence and for sustaining enzootic transmission in the absence of direct field vector infection data. The passage explicitly highlights this multi-approach confirmation, making this the most compelling finding in support of sustained cycles.

26.Option: The co-infection of a single host with multiple zoonotic trypanosomatid species, including one that successfully infected sand flies, suggests the potential for complex, multi-species transmission networks in the ecosystem
Evidence: Two individuals exhibited confirmed mixed infections supported by complementary diagnostic approaches. ID02 (D. albiventris) harbored both T. cruzi, detected in blood and lymph node samples, and T. lainsoni, identified by parasitological culture of blood and PCR from a tail skin fragment. ID09 (N. squamipes) was co-infected with L. infantum, detected through xenodiagnoses followed by PCR of fed sand flies, and T. lainsoni, isolated from blood culture.

These findings indicate that small mammals are exposed to, and may transiently harbor, zoonotic parasites at the wildlife-urban interface; however, given the reduced number of captured individuals and the absence of parallel vector sampling in this study, inferences regarding reservoir competence or sustained maintenance of transmission cycles in the study area must remain conservative.
Because these evaluations were beyond the scope of the present study, transmissibility remains undetermined, a common limitation in studies employing xenodiagnoses as a proxy for host infectiousness.
26.Rationale: Co-infections demonstrate ecological complexity and the possibility of multi-species networks, and the fact that one co-infected host yielded Leishmania detection in sand flies supports potential vector acquisition. However, the passage cautions that sample size is small, vector sampling is limited, and transmissibility remains undetermined when xenodiagnoses is the only evidence. Compared with the clear multi-method confirmation for T. cruzi in D. albiventris (Option 1), co-infection evidence is suggestive but not the most robust support for sustained transmission cycles given these stated limitations.

26.Option: The detection of T. lainsoni in both a D. albiventris and a N. squamipes individual, confirmed by multiple methods, indicates that this species is a key driver of zoonotic transmission in the urban-forest interface
Evidence: Trypanosoma lainsoni, with no known pathogenicity to humans, remains poorly characterized [40,41].
To date, no natural vector has been confirmed for this species.

The absence of T. lainsoni in both R. neglectus and L. longipalpis in our xenodiagnoses may reflect a degree of vector incompatibility or low parasitemia and limited parasite acquisition, although this remains inconclusive.
26.Rationale: Although T. lainsoni was detected in multiple hosts (expanding its known host range), the passage explicitly states it has "no known pathogenicity to humans," is "poorly characterized," and lacks a confirmed natural vector. The absence of T. lainsoni in xenodiagnoses of the tested vectors further weakens the case. Therefore it cannot be identified as a key driver of zoonotic transmission at the urban-forest interface based on the data presented.

26.Option: The high prevalence of trypanosomatid infections in small mammals (35.3%) across all three species suggests that the entire community functions as a reservoir for zoonotic transmission in the fragmented forest
Evidence: In this study, six of the 17 small mammals examined in the laboratory (35.3%) were naturally infected with trypanosomatids, including individuals of all three species captured.

Nonetheless, some limitations must be acknowledged. First, the limited sample size and representation of only three small mammal species restrict ecological inference and likely underestimate the diversity of trypanosomatids in the MT area.

Although the present findings are based on a limited number of hosts and do not allow robust inferences regarding reservoir competence or the long-term maintenance of transmission cycles, they provide evidence that small mammals inhabiting wildlife-urban interfaces are exposed to, and can harbor, zoonotic trypanosomatids of public health relevance.
26.Rationale: A 35.3% infection proportion across sampled individuals suggests substantial parasite occurrence and community exposure, which is suggestive of potential reservoir capacity. However, the authors explicitly caution that the limited sample size and restricted species representation "do not allow robust inferences regarding reservoir competence or the long-term maintenance of transmission cycles." Given these caveats, this finding is supportive but not the most convincing singular piece of evidence for sustained transmission cycles compared with the multi-method-confirmed T. cruzi infection in D. albiventris (Option 1).

27.Option: The high infection prevalence in T. vitticeps across multiple mesoregions indicates that the vector is a highly efficient reservoir, enabling sustained transmission and spatial spread of T. cruzi genotypes without requiring movement
Evidence: the total number of records in the period 2010–2020 were 2527 specimens: 997 (39.45%) were not infected and 1530 (60.55%) were infected by flagellated forms [35,41].
T. vitticeps is considered a secondary vector of T. cruzi due to the long interval between feeding and defecation [25], oral transmission remains possible given its high infection rates [10,11].
The origin of the high infection rates remains unclear, as no colonies, nymphs, or eggs were found in surrounding areas [10,25,41].

The prevalence of winged adults and the absence of nymphs reinforce this idea, suggesting that the flight capacity of T. vitticeps...facilitates long-distance dispersal, supporting Dario et al.’s hypothesis [10,11,41].
27.Rationale: Although the passage documents high infection prevalence in T. vitticeps, it explicitly describes the species as a secondary vector (long interval to defecation) and notes absence of local reproductive stages (no colonies, nymphs, or eggs). Those facts argue against treating the species as a highly efficient, self-sustaining reservoir that would spread genotypes without movement. Instead, the text emphasizes dispersal (flight of winged adults) as a mechanism for spatial spread, undermining the option’s claim that movement is unnecessary.

27.Option: The presence of dense vegetation (high NDVI) and high topographic diversity creates microhabitats that support the coexistence and transmission of multiple T. cruzi genotypes within localized enzootic cycles
Evidence: occurrences of T. vitticeps and its infections by T. cruzi (TcII, TcIII, TcIV and Z3) were recorded in areas with dense, healthy vegetation (NDVI with  ≥ 0.7), average altitude above 394.64 m (except for TcIII, which has an average altitude of its occurrences of 224.80 m) (S4 Table).
Topographic diversity further reflects ecosystem heterogeneity and the variety of topoclimatic niches that support higher biodiversity and species persistence under climate change [87,88].

The concentration of T. vitticeps and its infections ... suggests that vector movement may originate from areas with preserved vegetation (high NDVI values) and higher-altitude regions [41] characterized by greater topographic diversity (S2 and S4 Tables).
This scenario reflects the prevailing land-use and land-cover patterns in these areas, which are predominantly covered by forest and pasture [60].
27.Rationale: Dense vegetation and topographic diversity are clearly associated with suitability, coexistence, and localized enzootic cycles of multiple DTUs in the passage. However, the question asks which ecological factor most strongly supports the hypothesis that triatomine movement contributes to spatial spread across fragmented landscapes. Habitat heterogeneity supports local maintenance (coexistence) but does not directly indicate movement-driven spread between fragments. The passage points to dispersal mechanisms (e.g., wind-enhanced flight) as the primary support for movement-mediated spread, making this option less directly relevant to the specific hypothesis about movement enabling spatial spread.

27.Option: Wind-enhanced flight capacity of adult triatomines in mountainous regions enables long-distance dispersal and the spread of multiple T. cruzi genotypes across fragmented landscapes
Evidence: Wind has been identified as one of the factors influencing the flight displacement of triatomines, typically associated with low wind speeds and other factors such as temperature, humidity, and nutritional status [29,80,101–105].

The prevalence of winged adults and the absence of nymphs reinforce this idea, suggesting that the flight capacity of T. vitticeps, likely enhanced by the mountainous relief and prevailing air currents of the Central mesoregion, facilitates long-distance dispersal, supporting Dario et al.’s hypothesis [10,11,41].

Such displacement supports the concept of “Distantiae Transmission” of T. cruzi, previously attributed to anthropogenic movement of triatomines [106], but here possibly driven by abiotic environmental factors that enable the passive dispersal of T. vitticeps to new areas.

Thus, wind speed appears to be a key factor determining the dispersal capacity of infected T. vitticeps in the Espírito Santo, representing a potential novel mechanism for the long-distance transmission of T. cruzi.
27.Rationale: The passage explicitly identifies wind (and mountain-driven air currents) as promoting flight displacement and long-distance dispersal of adult T. vitticeps, links that dispersal to the concept of distant transmission of T. cruzi, and states that wind speed is a key factor determining dispersal capacity. These statements most directly support the hypothesis that triatomine movement drives spatial spread of distinct T. cruzi genotypes across a fragmented landscape.

27.Option: High mammal species richness in forested areas provides a reservoir for multiple T. cruzi genotypes, enabling their persistence and spatial spread through host movement
Evidence: Decision tree analyses (Fig 7 and Tables 4 and 5) consistently identified wind speed, mammal richness, and maximum temperature as the variables for classifying infected T. vitticeps, highlighting the relevance of these explanatory variables in field planning.

Mammalian diversity and maximum temperature are important variables in vector dynamics, as ectothermic triatomines exhibit increased activity, reproduction, and feeding frequency at higher temperatures, highlighting their combined role in shaping population ecology [98].
This indicates that even with limited TcIII data, potential presence locations can be inferred.
In contrast, the North Coast and Northwest mesoregions... favor generalist species like Didelphis and bats, which likely sustain the T. cruzi cycle [11,23,94,95].
27.Rationale: Mammal richness is implicated as important for maintenance of T. cruzi and appears among variables classifying infected triatomines, supporting reservoir roles for wild hosts. However, the question targets evidence that movement (triatomine dispersal) contributes to spatial spread across fragmented landscapes. Host richness suggests local persistence and potential for local transmission, but the passage emphasizes wind-enhanced triatomine dispersal as the principal mechanism enabling spread between fragments. Thus mammal richness supports maintenance, not movement-driven spatial spread as directly as wind-mediated dispersal.

27.Option: Deforestation and land-use change increase the likelihood of triatomine invasion into human dwellings, leading to the accidental spread of T. cruzi genotypes through human-mediated transport
Evidence: NDVI is a classical indicator of vegetation health and density... an indication of anthropogenic disturbance - a relevant factor when interpreting triatomine foraging behavior, since deforestation drives these insects to seek alternative food sources due to altered local biodiversity [26,34,86].

The North Coast and Northwest, characterized by lower altitudes... have undergone intense landscape fragmentation and deforestation, which affect the dynamics of mammal hosts and triatomine populations by restricting them to remnant forest patches [26,90].
In any case, the North Coast remains an ecologically distinctive region, favoring generalist species like Didelphis and bats, which likely sustain the T. cruzi cycle [11,23,94,95].

Such displacement supports the concept of “Distantiae Transmission” of T. cruzi, previously attributed to anthropogenic movement of triatomines [106], but here possibly driven by abiotic environmental factors that enable the passive dispersal of T. vitticeps to new areas.
27.Rationale: The passage documents that deforestation and land-use change increase home invasions and alter host/vector dynamics, and it notes that distant (anthropogenic) movement has been previously suggested. However, the authors highlight abiotic wind-mediated dispersal as a more strongly supported mechanism for long-distance spread in Espírito Santo. While deforestation plausibly increases invasion risk and could enable accidental (human-mediated) transport, the text treats anthropogenic transport as a previous explanation and emphasizes wind-enhanced triatomine movement as the stronger, novel ecological factor supporting spatial spread of genotypes, making this option less supported as the 'most strongly' relevant factor.

28.Option: The high prevalence of Colpodella spp. in Hy. excavatum ticks from livestock-rearing districts, combined with evidence of human and vertebrate infection and tick-mediated transmission, suggests this tick species may act as a reservoir for a zoonotic pathogen
Evidence: This protozoan was primarily found in Hy. excavatum collected from Buner and Kohistan, with prevalence rates of 8.98% (15/167) and 5.48% (9/164), respectively (Table 3).
Colpodella spp., a free-living microorganism closely related to apicomplexan parasites, represents an evolutionary bridge between free-living protozoa and parasitic apicomplexans [27,28,18].

Colpodella spp. have been reported to infect vertebrates (e.g., Amur tiger, horse) and humans,which are thought to possibly be transmitted by infected Rhipicephalus microplus, Dermacentor everestianus, and D. nuttalli ticks [29,30,31].
The findings of this study make a case for expanded surveillance of this microorganism in Hy. anatolicum ticks as a possible carrier of Colpodella spp.
28.Rationale: Detection of Colpodella spp. at appreciable prevalence (8.98% and 5.48%) in Hy. excavatum from livestock-rearing districts, combined with independent evidence in the passage that Colpodella can infect vertebrates and humans and is thought to be tick-transmitted, provides strong support that that particular tick species (and the tick community) could act as a reservoir or carrier of a zoonotic agent. The study authors themselves recommend expanded surveillance of Colpodella in ticks, consistent with reservoir potential.

28.Option: The high overall infection rate of 5.67% across all tick species supports the hypothesis that ticks in livestock-rearing communities may serve as reservoirs for zoonotic pathogens
Evidence: Of the 1,305 collected ticks, 510 were selected for molecular screening using PCR. ... Out of these, 74 ticks tested positive for at least one pathogen, resulting in an overall infection rate of 5.67%.
28.Rationale: While the overall infection rate (5.67%) shows that pathogens are present in the tick population, this aggregate metric is relatively modest and non-specific. Reservoir inference is stronger when specific tick species show consistent, localized, and reasonably high pathogen prevalence or when there is corroborating evidence of transmission to vertebrates/humans. The overall rate alone does not identify which species sustain infections or demonstrate ecologic/epidemiologic linkage needed to support a reservoir role.

28.Option: The presence of R. hoogstraalii in Hae. punctata ticks from Karak, a district with high livestock density, supports the hypothesis that this tick species may serve as a reservoir for a zoonotic pathogen
Evidence: The highest pathogen prevalence observed in the study was in Karak, where Hae. punctata carried R. hoogstraalii at a rate of 14.28% (12/84), marking the district as a hotspot for rickettsial infections.
Here we describe the first report of R. hoogstraalii detected in Hae. punctata in Pakistan.
28.Rationale: A relatively high, localized prevalence (14.28%) of R. hoogstraalii in a specific tick species (Hae. punctata) and the identification of Karak as a hotspot provide stronger, species-specific evidence supporting that Hae. punctata could serve as a reservoir or important carrier in that livestock-rearing area. The novelty of this detection in Pakistan further supports epidemiologic significance and need for follow-up to assess reservoir competence and zoonotic risk.

28.Option: The detection of P. rettgeri in Hy. excavatum ticks from Bannu, despite the possibility of contamination from host blood meals, indicates that this tick species may serve as a reservoir for a zoonotic pathogen
Evidence: In Bannu, Hy. excavatum was found to harbor P. rettgeri, with a prevalence of 5.83% (8/137), suggesting the emergence of this bacterium as a potential zoonotic agent.

First, due to the engorged status of some of the collected ticks, there is a possibility that the detected pathogens particularly P. rettgeri originated from the goat host's blood meal rather than representing true tick infections. This raises the concern of environmental or host-derived contamination, especially in the case of P. rettgeri, which is known to be an opportunistic pathogen in diverse environments.
28.Rationale: Although P. rettgeri was detected in Hy. excavatum, the authors explicitly note the possibility that P. rettgeri detections may reflect contamination from host blood meals rather than true tick infection. That caveat substantially weakens inference that Hy. excavatum is a reservoir for P. rettgeri; additional evidence (pathogen localization within tick tissues, repeated detections in unfed ticks, or transmission experiments) would be required to support reservoir status.

29.Option: Autonomic nervous system dysfunction was present in the absence of clinical symptoms and structural cardiac abnormalities, indicating it occurs prior to detectable heart damage
Evidence: In the acute phase, symptoms were non-specific, including fever, myalgia, and malaise. Epigastric pain was reported by one patient. No cardiological symptoms were reported by any patient.
Echocardiogram results indicated normal ejection fraction and cavity diameters in all patients.

Regarding heart rate variability, the results of analyses performed in the acute phase of CD, without treatment, for both long-term (Holter methodology) and short-term (5 minutes) periods are described in Table 2 and Table 3.
In the acute phase of Chagas Disease, alterations were observed in the 24-hour time-domain variables, specifically in SDANN (p-value = 0.04; rrb = 0.35) and SDNN (p-value = 0.04; rrb = 0,29).

In the short-term period (5 minutes), the following altered indices were identified: heart rate (HR) with an increase in the acute phase group (p-value = 0.01; rrb = 0.47); SDNN – reflecting a sympathovagal imbalance (p-value = 0.04; rrb = 0.38); rMSSD – an index influenced by the parasympathetic autonomic nervous system (p-value = 0.02; rrb = 0.44)
Several studies have demonstrated that autonomic dysfunction precedes the development of ventricular dysfunction and heart failure.
29.Rationale: The strongest support for the hypothesis that autonomic dysfunction precedes structural cardiac damage is the coexistence of objective autonomic abnormalities (multiple altered HRV indices in both long- and short-term measures) together with no cardiological symptoms and normal echocardiographic structural findings in all patients. The passage also explicitly notes prior evidence that autonomic dysfunction can precede ventricular dysfunction, which directly supports the precursor hypothesis.

29.Option: The normalization of heart rate variability after benznidazole treatment, coupled with persistent echocardiographic normality, suggests that autonomic dysfunction is a transient phenomenon unrelated to long-term cardiac risk
Evidence: In the post-treatment phase, all measured parameters exhibited sustained normalization, indicating a restoration of autonomic nervous system function.
Echocardiogram results indicated normal ejection fraction and cavity diameters in all patients.
Although heart rate variability assessment indices were normalized, a parasympathetic inhibition response was observed in the recovery phase of the exercise stress test.
Several studies have demonstrated that autonomic dysfunction precedes the development of ventricular dysfunction and heart failure.
Thus, our study demonstrates a trend in the autonomic nervous system response, opening perspectives for further studies in the population with Chagas disease.

Although the normalization of heart rate variability parameters could serve as an additional justification for the favorable clinical course in individuals treated for Acute Chagas Disease (ACD) at FMT-HVD, the autonomic nervous system dysfunction observed during the acute phase still highlights the need for longer-term follow-up of this population to assess the long-term progression and outcomes of Chagas disease in our region.
29.Rationale: While HRV indices normalized after treatment and echocardiography remained normal, the passage does not support concluding that autonomic dysfunction is unrelated to long-term risk. The authors note persistent parasympathetic inhibition on exercise recovery, cite literature that autonomic dysfunction can precede ventricular dysfunction, and explicitly call for longer-term follow-up. Thus the option overstates the implication of transient normalization and contradicts the paper's caution about long-term risk.

Thus the claim that model prediction is "validated by high correlation" with livestock and that livestock are reliable amplifying hosts for all three viruses is not supported by the quoted model results, which show only limited livestock influence on virus suitability overall.

43.Option: The model's prediction of virus presence is biologically plausible because the identified vectors are known to transmit other arboviruses, supporting inference of shared transmission pathways across viruses
Evidence: The best predictors of the viruses were the ecological niches of their mosquito vectors, a finding corroborated by models of Dengue using its vector, Ae. aegypti [57].

The vectors we analyzed are also important vectors for other viruses of public health importance, i.e., Ae. circumluteolus (Spondweni, Zika, Lebombo, Kedougou, Bunyamwera, Ndumu, Pongola and RVF); Ae. mcintoshi (Babanki, Ndumu, Bunyamwera, Ngari, Pongola, RVF); Cx. univittatus (West Nile, Usutu, WSLV, RVF); Cx. pipiens (West Nile, Usutu, Semliki Forest, RVF, Japanese Encephalitis, Venezuelan Equine Encephalitis), Ma. africana (Spondweni, Usutu, RVF) [4,95,96].

The diversity of niches suitable for these vectors implies that where suitable blood meals or potential hosts (bird, livestock, or human) are present, the transmission, maintenance, and spread of multiple arboviral diseases is likely [4].
43.Rationale: The passage explicitly states that virus models were driven by the ecological niches of their mosquito vectors and that those vectors are known to transmit a range of other arboviruses. This makes the virus presence predictions biologically plausible and supports inferring shared or analogous transmission pathways (e.g., similar vector-mediated processes) across viruses, even if the models do not prove specific transmission events.

43.Option: The model's prediction of virus presence is inferred from the consistent detection of all three viruses in the same mosquito species, indicating a shared transmission cycle across Africa.
Evidence: WSLV has been detected from multiple mosquito taxa, including several Aedes (Ae), Anopheles, Culex (Cx), and Mansonia (Ma) species, but its main vectors are freshwater breeding Aedes species, notably, Ae. circumluteolus, Ae. mcintoshi and Ae. caballus [4,9,10].

SINV isolations are dominated by Cx. univittatus and Cx. pipiens in Africa, while in Europe Cx. torrentium/Cx. pipiens, Cx. perexiguus, Culiseta morsistans, Ae. cinereus and Ae. Ochlerotatus caballus play important roles [17,24,53,54].
Field and molecular studies have detected MIDV in several mosquito genera, including Aedes and Culex, supporting the likelihood of a multi-vector system [32].
We modeled habitat suitability for three viruses (WSLV, SINV, and MIDV) and five mosquito vectors (Ae. circumluteolus, Ae. mcintoshi, Cx. pipiens, Cx. univittatus and Ma. africana).

Our virus models did not include niche models for all known mosquito-virus detections; instead, focal vector species were chosen. We acknowledge that omitting other species could bias spatial predictions where those other suspected vectors dominate local transmission cycles.
43.Rationale: The passage describes different primary or dominant vector taxa for each virus (WSLV associated with floodwater Aedes; SINV dominated by Culex species; MIDV detected in multiple genera). It also notes a multi-vector system and that the modeling used selected focal vectors rather than showing consistent detection of all three viruses in the same mosquito species. Therefore the assertion of a shared transmission cycle across Africa based on consistent detection in the same species is not supported.

43.Option: The model's prediction of virus presence is supported by the spatial overlap between vector suitability and human population density, indicating that human exposure risk is directly driven by vector abundance.
Evidence: We overlaid the combined presence-absence model outputs of the three viruses with gridded human population density across Africa for each scenario.

Under future climate scenarios (SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5), environmentally suitable areas for low to moderate certainty of virus presence were projected to expand into increasingly populated suburban and urban settings, illustrated by yellow and green tones (Fig 8).

While this does not imply increased transmission risk per se, it positions human population as another important attribute of ecological transitions that could modify virus presence and human exposure.
ecological suitability maps are intended to represent ecological conditions associated with documented virus occurrence rather than realized transmission or infection risk.
43.Rationale: Although the models show spatial overlap between ecological suitability (vector/virus presence) and human population and note expansion of suitable areas into more populated settings, the authors explicitly caution that ecological suitability or overlap does not imply realized transmission risk. Thus it is not correct to conclude directly that human exposure risk is driven solely or directly by vector abundance based on these models.

43.Option: The model's prediction of virus presence is strengthened by the high predictive performance of the vector niche models, which confirms that the same mosquito species are competent vectors for all three viruses.
Evidence: Final models produced using the best candidate model settings resulted in higher mean AUC ratios (Range = 1.67 - 1.97) implying improved fitness of training data and better predictive performance (S4 Table).
However, detecting a virus in a mosquito does not necessarily establish it as a competent vector in viral maintenance.
Much of this evidence is based on field isolations rather than controlled vector competence studies [4,32,33,55].

Our virus models did not include niche models for all known mosquito-virus detections; instead, focal vector species were chosen. We acknowledge that omitting other species could bias spatial predictions where those other suspected vectors dominate local transmission cycles.
43.Rationale: While the passage reports good predictive performance metrics for the niche models, the authors explicitly state that field detections do not confirm vector competence and that controlled vector competence data are scarce. The high model performance supports ecological plausibility of vector distributions but does not confirm that the same mosquito species are competent vectors for all three viruses; competence requires experimental evidence beyond niche-model fit.

44.Option: Genotype K replaced genotype J because it was more resistant to antiviral drugs used during the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic
Evidence: These antivirals fall into two main categories: one targets viral proteins—primarily viral enzymes—to disrupt the viral life cycle, while the other targets host proteins involved in viral entry and replication, such as host cell receptors or proteases [34].
These antivirals ... act on key viral enzymes such as the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp/nsp12).

some studies [41–43] indicate that coronaviruses tend to accumulate mutations more readily under drug pressure. Therefore, during the pandemic, the widespread use of broad-spectrum antiviral agents may have indirectly contributed to the accelerated evolution of structurally related viruses, such as HCoV-OC43.
44.Rationale: The passage only raises antiviral drug pressure as a possible indirect contributor to accelerated evolution and describes antivirals that target conserved enzymes; it does not provide evidence that genotype K specifically acquired antiviral resistance or that drug resistance drove genotype replacement. The text frames antivirals as a potential, indirect factor rather than the demonstrated mechanism for K replacing J.

44.Option: Genotype K outcompeted genotype J due to increased transmission efficiency from higher replication rates in the absence of SARS-CoV-2 competition
Evidence: SARS-CoV-2 shows greater transmission efficiency than HCoV-OC43. SARS-CoV-2 spread rapidly and globally upon its emergence.

competition between the two viruses for ecological niches may lead to competition for the same host or biological resources, which is exacerbated by the widespread implementation of social quarantine measures [25,26].
These evolutionary adaptations likely contribute to viral persistence and ecological competitiveness.
44.Rationale: The passage emphasizes competition between viruses and highlights adaptive mutations that enhance binding, fusion, and transmission as drivers of genotype success, not a scenario of ‘‘absence of SARS-CoV-2 competition’’ leading to higher replication rates. There is no direct evidence presented that genotype K rose because SARS-CoV-2 was absent or that simple higher replication rate in the absence of SARS-CoV-2 explains the replacement.

44.Option: Genotype K became dominant due to a higher rate of recombination events that generated novel genotypes with enhanced fitness
Evidence: recombination analysis identified only a few potential recombinant sequences, all of which were sampled before the COVID-19 pandemic, and SimPlot validation did not reveal clear or stable parental fragment exchanges (detailed information is in S1 File).
Therefore, the impact of recombination on the BEAST-based estimation of nucleotide substitution rates is expected to be minimal.
44.Rationale: The authors explicitly report only a few potential recombinant sequences (all sampled pre-pandemic) and conclude that recombination's impact is expected to be minimal. Thus the passage does not support increased recombination as the mechanism for post-pandemic dominance of genotype K.

44.Option: Genotype K became dominant due to a higher mutation rate in the spike gene that increased genetic diversity and adaptive potential
Evidence: The acceleration was most pronounced in the S gene, with nucleotide substitution rates increasing from 2.3757 × 10 ⁻ ⁴ (95% HPD: 9.4851 × 10 ⁻ ⁵, 3.9034 × 10 ⁻ ⁴) to 8.9403 × 10 ⁻ ⁴ (95% HPD: 4.9075 × 10 ⁻ ⁴, 1.3053 × 10 ⁻ ³) (S2 Table and Fig 2A-2D).
Comparison of total nucleotide substitution rates across the S, RdRp, and N genes revealed that the S gene exhibited the highest rate.
within genotype K, sequences sampled after 2020 accumulated more substitutions compared with those sampled before 2020, whereas genotype J exhibited the reverse pattern (S1 Fig).
44.Rationale: While the passage documents an accelerated substitution (mutation) rate in the spike (S) gene of genotype K after the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic — which could increase genetic diversity and potential for adaptation — the authors emphasize selection acting on adaptive spike mutations under immune (cross-reactive) pressure as the proximate driver of genotype replacement. Thus increased mutation rate is a contributing factor but the passage points to adaptive selection (immune-driven) as the key mechanism for the genotype shift, so this option alone is incomplete as the primary explanation.

44.Option: Genotype K gained a selective advantage through adaptive mutations in the spike protein that enhance receptor binding and immune evasion under cross-reactive host immunity
Evidence: Under selection pressure, adaptive mutations at key amino acid sites in the spike and nucleocapsid proteins of HCoV-OC43 may enhance the virus’s ability to recognize and bind to host sialic acid receptors, facilitate membrane fusion and viral assembly, and promote efficient host cell entry.

Positively selected sites were found only in the S and N proteins of genotype K (behaving as genotype I at the N gene level) ... Seventeen positively selected sites ... were detected in the S protein of genotype K

The results of historical evolution analysis showed that amino acid mutations at positively selected sites ... were observed at tree nodes or within subclades corresponding to sequences collected after the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic.
immune pressure resulting from cross-reactivity between SARS-CoV-2 and HCoV-OC43 in host cells may serve as a driving force for the accelerated evolution of HCoV-OC43.
44.Rationale: The passage provides multiple lines of evidence that genotype K accumulated positively selected (adaptive) mutations in the S (spike) protein after the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, that these mutations are predicted to enhance receptor binding, fusion, and possibly immune evasion, and that cross-reactive immunity from SARS-CoV-2 could provide the selection pressure. Together these statements identify adaptive spike mutations under cross-reactive immune pressure as the most likely mechanism for the post-pandemic shift to genotype K dominance.

46.Option: The absence of a formal surveillance system in northern regions leads to underreporting, which artificially reduces the observed prevalence compared to southern and insular regions
Evidence: While cystic echinococcosis is a notifiable parasitic infectious disease in Italy, limitations in the national health system data collection and notification reports result in underestimation and misinterpretation of the disease’s epidemiological situation, which reinforces the mistaken belief that CE poses minimal health risks.
The absence of a formal surveillance system, diagnostic ambiguity and variability in regional reporting contribute to persistent challenges in estimating the true burden of the disease [7,9,10].
The southern and insular regions accounted for 50.6% (n = 1,348) of the total cystic echinococcosis.

These findings highlight the persistence of hyperendemic foci in certain macroregions, which reflected socio-economic and agricultural factors, particularly in areas where extensive sheep farming is widely practised [17].
46.Rationale: Although the passage states that absence of a formal surveillance system and underreporting affect estimates nationally, it does not attribute the north–south disparity specifically to worse surveillance in the north. Instead, the passage directly links higher prevalence in southern/insular regions to persistent hyperendemic foci and extensive sheep farming. Therefore the surveillance-absence explanation for the geographic disparity is not the most direct explanation supported by the text.

46.Option: The higher proportion of elderly patients in southern and insular regions, who are more vulnerable to severe disease, leads to increased hospitalization and thus higher observed prevalence in those areas
Evidence: The vast majority of patients (>90%) were adults, including 20.4% young adults (25–44 years), 30.2% middle aged adults (45–64 years) and 41.1% senior adults (over 65 years).
Patients over the age of 65 accounted for 70% of the mortalities.
The southern and insular regions accounted for 50.6% (n = 1,348) of the total cystic echinococcosis.

These findings highlight the persistence of hyperendemic foci in certain macroregions, which reflected socio-economic and agricultural factors, particularly in areas where extensive sheep farming is widely practised [17].
46.Rationale: The passage documents that most cases are adults and that elderly patients account for most in-hospital deaths, but it does not state that a higher proportion of elderly in the southern/insular regions explains regional prevalence differences. Instead, the text attributes geographic disparity to agricultural practices and the sheep-dog transmission cycle. Thus the elderly-proportion/hospitalization explanation is not the most directly supported factor.

46.Option: The lower hospitalization rates in northern regions due to better access to outpatient care and earlier diagnosis reduce the observed prevalence of CE in those areas
Evidence: There are various limitations to this approach, since asymptomatic patients may be diagnosed accidentally or in an outpatient setting, or even may not require hospitalisation, thus de facto eluding the HDRs reporting system.

As already described [5], we observed a lower prevalence of CE in the northern regions of Italy, particularly in the North West (0.34/105 inhabitants), that may suggest a less effective E. granulosus life cycle perpetuation as well as a higher migratory pressure in these areas.

These findings highlight the persistence of hyperendemic foci in certain macroregions, which reflected socio-economic and agricultural factors, particularly in areas where extensive sheep farming is widely practised [17].
46.Rationale: While the passage notes that outpatient diagnoses and non-hospitalised cases can escape hospital discharge records, it does not present evidence that northern regions specifically have lower hospitalization rates because of better outpatient care or earlier diagnosis. The passage instead proposes ecological explanations (less effective parasite life cycle, migratory pressure) and emphasizes extensive sheep farming in the south/islands as the driver of higher prevalence. Therefore this option is not the best-supported explanation.

46.Option: The persistence of extensive sheep farming and the associated sheep-dog transmission cycle in southern and insular regions sustains long-term exposure, leading to higher historical infection rates reflected in current adult case distribution
Evidence: The southern and insular regions accounted for 50.6% (n = 1,348) of the total cystic echinococcosis.

These findings highlight the persistence of hyperendemic foci in certain macroregions, which reflected socio-economic and agricultural factors, particularly in areas where extensive sheep farming is widely practised [17].

The significance of the sheep-dog cycle in the transmission patterns of the parasite is well established, ensuring the perpetuation of the life cycle through at-risk practices including illegal slaughter, feeding dogs with raw viscera and unappropriated carcasses disposal.

From a demographic perspective, and in line with other researches [9,26,27], more than 90% of patients belonged to adult age groups... This pattern reflects the long incubation period, the low mortality rate of the disease and the slow development of CE cysts before clinical manifestation.
46.Rationale: The passage explicitly links higher prevalence in southern and insular regions to persistent hyperendemic foci driven by socio-economic and agricultural factors, especially extensive sheep farming and the sheep-dog cycle (illegal slaughter, feeding dogs raw viscera). The predominance of adult cases is explained by long incubation and slow cyst development, consistent with historical exposure in these areas. Thus this factor most directly explains the geographic disparity described.

46.Option: The higher proportion of foreign-born residents in northern regions, who may have acquired the infection in their country of origin, explains the lower prevalence of CE in those areas compared to southern and insular regions
Evidence: Fig 2 illustrates the nationality of the estimated human CE patients in Italy, reflecting the higher presence of foreigners in the northern regions (North West: 41%; North East: 57%), compared to the Centre (35%), the South (18%), and the Islands (3%).

As already described [5], we observed a lower prevalence of CE in the northern regions of Italy, particularly in the North West (0.34/105 inhabitants), that may suggest a less effective E. granulosus life cycle perpetuation as well as a higher migratory pressure in these areas.

Indeed, a higher proportion of CE patients of foreign nationality are living in the northern regions of Italy (52% Italians, 48% foreigners). The North East, in particular, represents a better economic opportunities and a long-term settlement for foreign populations [24,25].
46.Rationale: The passage notes a higher proportion of foreign patients in northern regions and acknowledges they may have acquired infection abroad, but this does not explain why the northern regions have lower overall prevalence compared to the south/islands. If anything, imported cases complicate interpretation but do not account for lower endemic transmission. The text identifies reduced perpetuation of the parasite life cycle and the lack of extensive sheep farming in the north as the more direct explanations. Therefore this option is not supported as the primary reason for the geographic disparity.

47.Option: The positive correlation between placental and maternal egg counts supports the hypothesis that placental schistosomiasis is a direct consequence of ongoing maternal infection and contributes to adverse birth outcomes through systemic inflammation
Evidence: Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient indicated a positive correlation between placental egg count and maternal egg count (Spearman’s rho = 0.72). However, even if this dose-response effect is biologically plausible it should be interpreted with caution since it might be due to sampling variation (p = 0.17) owing to the very small sample size (n = 5) in this analysis.
Schistosomiasis has been linked to adverse birth outcomes such as prematurity, low birth weight and stillbirth, but underlying mechanisms are not yet fully understood.
47.Rationale: Although the passage reports a positive correlation (Spearman’s rho = 0.72) between placental and maternal egg counts, the authors explicitly caution that this finding may be due to sampling variation (p = 0.17) and very small sample size (n = 5). Thus, the correlation is weak evidence in this study and does not strongly support the claim that placental schistosomiasis independently contributes to adverse birth outcomes via systemic inflammation. Instead, it mainly indicates that placental egg burden covaries with maternal egg burden, and the study authors warn about overinterpreting this result.

47.Option: The detection of placental schistosomiasis in women without detectable urinary schistosomiasis suggests a distinct pathological process that may independently contribute to adverse birth outcomes
Evidence: Interestingly, there was also one positive case of PS (5%; 1/20; 95% CI: 0.1-24.9%) among women without S. haematobium infection.

However, urine screening for S. haematobium was only done on one day, while screening on three consecutive days could have increased the diagnostic sensitivity. This is even demonstrated by our findings since there was one case of PS in a woman with a negative light microscopic result.
This suggests that PS could be an underestimated phenomenon in highly endemic regions and warrants further investigations of its implications for mother-and-child health.
47.Rationale: The study did find a case of placental schistosomiasis in a woman who tested negative by urine microscopy. However, the authors attribute this more plausibly to insufficient sensitivity of the single-day urine test rather than to a distinct pathological process that is independent of maternal infection. The passage explicitly notes the limited sensitivity of single-sample urine microscopy and that the finding ‘is even demonstrated by our findings’ as an example of diagnostic limitations. Therefore, the evidence does not strongly support a distinct, independent pathological process; it more strongly supports under-detection of maternal infection.

47.Option: The higher prevalence of placental schistosomiasis among infected women compared to uninfected women indicates that maternal infection intensity directly drives placental pathology and adverse birth outcomes
Evidence: Among infected women with available placental samples, the prevalence of PS was 14.3% (4/28; 95% CI: 4.0-32.7%), whereas among the women from the non-infected, control group with available placental samples the prevalence of PS was 5% (1/20; 95% CI: 0.1-24.9%).
Among women with S. haematobium infection, the egg count in urine ranged from 1 to 870 eggs per 10 mL. The median egg count was 50 (IQR: 8 – 113).
47.Rationale: A higher PS prevalence among infected versus uninfected women shows that maternal infection is associated with placental involvement, but this supports the idea that maternal infection leads to placental pathology rather than demonstrating that PS contributes to adverse birth outcomes beyond maternal infection effects. The option asserts a direct causal link from maternal infection intensity to adverse outcomes; the study does not provide evidence that PS adds independent risk beyond maternal infection, nor does it establish that intensity drives adverse outcomes. Thus this option overstates what the data support.

47.Option: The presence of placental schistosomiasis in women with negative urine tests suggests that the current diagnostic method for maternal infection is insufficient and that placental involvement may be a more accurate indicator of disease burden and risk for adverse outcomes
Evidence: Interestingly, there was also one positive case of PS (5%; 1/20; 95% CI: 0.1-24.9%) among women without S. haematobium infection.

However, urine screening for S. haematobium was only done on one day, while screening on three consecutive days could have increased the diagnostic sensitivity. This is even demonstrated by our findings since there was one case of PS in a woman with a negative light microscopic result.

Conventional histopathology has limited diagnostic sensitivity because only small tissue fragments can be examined due to feasibility aspects. The improved KOH-based tissue maceration technique addresses these limitations by allowing efficient examination of larger placental tissue volumes, thereby increasing the likelihood of detecting eggs [15].
This suggests that PS could be an underestimated phenomenon in highly endemic regions and warrants further investigations of its implications for mother-and-child health.
47.Rationale: The study’s detection of PS in a participant whose urine microscopy was negative, together with the authors’ discussion that single-sample urine microscopy has limited sensitivity and that improved maceration detects more eggs, supports the idea that placental examination may reveal disease not captured by standard maternal screening. If placental involvement is missed by routine maternal diagnostics, then PS could represent additional, under-recognized disease burden that might relate to adverse outcomes independent of what maternal urine tests indicate. This diagnostic-gap finding most strongly supports the hypothesis that PS could contribute to adverse birth outcomes beyond the effects identified by maternal infection status alone.

47.Option: The detection of placental schistosomiasis in women with low-intensity maternal infection suggests that even mild parasitism can lead to placental inflammation and adverse birth outcomes
Evidence: Among women with S. haematobium infection, the egg count in urine ranged from 1 to 870 eggs per 10 mL. The median egg count was 50 (IQR: 8 – 113).
Approximately 15% of women with S. haematobium infection detected in urine also had PS.

Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient indicated a positive correlation between placental egg count and maternal egg count (Spearman’s rho = 0.72). However, even if this dose-response effect is biologically plausible it should be interpreted with caution since it might be due to sampling variation (p = 0.17) owing to the very small sample size (n = 5) in this analysis.
47.Rationale: The passage does not present clear evidence that PS occurred specifically in women with low-intensity maternal infections; egg counts varied widely and the sample of placental positives is very small. The authors also caution about the small sample size and potential sampling variation, undermining assertions about effects at low intensity. Therefore, the claim that detection of PS in low-intensity infections demonstrates that even mild parasitism leads to placental inflammation and adverse outcomes is not supported by the data presented.

48.Option: The co-occurrence of multiple chronic symptoms such as bowel and bladder dysfunction, which requires individuals to develop comprehensive daily management routines
Evidence: Typical symptoms of HAM/TSP include chronic spastic paraparesis-induced gait disorders, weakness of the lower limbs, bladder disturbance, constipation, and sensory symptoms, such as tingling, pins and needles, and burning [8].

Attempts to control bowel dysfunction are described by the strategies “Undertaking efforts to maintain bowel movement,” “Understanding the effects of laxatives,” and “Self-adjusting laxative dosage regimen.”
Attempts to control bladder dysfunction are described by the strategies “Seeking ways to control urination,” and “Excreting residual urine according to the rule of thumb.”

three characteristics of HAM/TSP – lack of an established curative treatment, low social awareness of the disease, and its infectious nature – had a significant impact on the self-management of individuals with HAM/TSP.
48.Rationale: The passage provides clear evidence that multiple concurrent symptoms (bladder disturbance, constipation, gait problems) drive the development of comprehensive daily management routines (quotes 1–3). However, the question asks about factors that influence development of strategies that address both personal health and social consequences. While symptom co-occurrence explains the need for detailed personal health management, the passage explicitly attributes social-consequence–related self-management to other characteristics (lack of awareness and infectious nature), not merely to symptom co-occurrence (quote 4). Therefore this option is incomplete as the primary factor affecting both personal and social aspects.

48.Option: The lack of public awareness about the disease, which leads individuals to develop strategies to gain social understanding and reduce stigma
Evidence: three characteristics of HAM/TSP – lack of an established curative treatment, low social awareness of the disease, and its infectious nature – had a significant impact on the self-management of individuals with HAM/TSP.
Specifically, HAM/TSP is not socially recognized and is likely to be misunderstood because of the interindividual variations in symptoms.
The lack of public awareness of HAM/TSP necessitates the incorporation of self-management strategies right from the time that an individual is diagnosed with HAM/TSP.
Because HAM/TSP is an infectious disease, stigma toward viral infections may arise.

Receiving the required support. People with HAM/TSP approached and used available official support and informal support from family members and others. ... “Realizing to be understood by those around one” refers to the realization that the disease condition of HAM/TSP and their health situation as it related to HAM/TSP are understood by those around them.
48.Rationale: The passage explicitly identifies low social awareness as one of three key characteristics shaping self-management and states that lack of public awareness 'necessitates' incorporating strategies from diagnosis onward (quotes 1 and 3). It also links low recognition to misunderstanding and stigma (quotes 2 and 4) and describes concrete self-management behaviors aimed at gaining understanding and support from others (quote 5). Thus lack of public awareness is directly implicated in development of strategies that address both personal health management and social consequences (understanding, stigma reduction).

48.Option: The presence of progressive neurological symptoms, which drives individuals to seek specialized medical care and develop strategies to maintain physical function
Evidence: As people with HAM/TSP approached the stage where they had trouble walking because of progressive motor disability, they recognized the need for alternative means of mobility besides walking and, depending on their individual conditions, acquired wheelchairs or a means to enable manual driving.

“Recognizing the need for physical activity” refers to the recognition of the need to intentionally move or rehabilitate the body to maintain muscle strength and stop the progression of gait disturbances. “Training to maintain motor function” refers to receiving regular professional rehabilitation or performing independent exercise.
Ensuring medical treatment by HAM/TSP specialist. People with HAM/TSP are eager to be seen and treated by HAM/TSP specialists, and they act to ensure this.
48.Rationale: Progressive neurological symptoms clearly drive self-management focused on maintaining physical function and seeking specialized care (quotes 1–3). However, the question asks which factor most likely influences strategies that address both personal health and social consequences. The passage indicates that social consequences (stigma, need for social understanding, concern for relatives) stem particularly from low awareness and the infectious nature of the disease, rather than from progressive symptoms alone. Therefore while this factor explains personal health strategies well, it does not by itself account for the social-consequence dimension, so it is not the best answer.

48.Option: The infectious nature of the disease, which necessitates strategies that address both personal symptom management and the risk of transmission to others
Evidence: three characteristics of HAM/TSP – lack of an established curative treatment, low social awareness of the disease, and its infectious nature – had a significant impact on the self-management of individuals with HAM/TSP.
As HAM/TSP is an infectious disease, stigma toward viral infections may arise.

Concern about the impact of HTLV-1 infection on close relatives. As HAM/TSP is an infectious disease that is caused by HTLV-1, one of the self-management strategies for their chronic conditions involves “Concern about the impact of HTLV-1 infection on close relatives,” such as informing a close relative of the possibility of their becoming infected with HAM/TSP or checking the results of HTLV-1 antibody tests on them.

This characteristic self-management strategy of people with HAM/TSP may include two intentions. The first is the proactive intention to prevent further spread of HTLV-1 infection through infection prevention actions. Preventing the spread of HTLV-1 reduces the risk of HAM/TSP and other related diseases for close relative. The second aim was to minimize misconceptions about HTLV-1 infection and its associated impact on relationships with others and social life.
48.Rationale: The passage explicitly lists infectiousness as one of three central characteristics shaping self-management (quote 1) and describes how it produces both stigma and concrete concerns about transmission to relatives (quotes 2–3). It further explains that self-management responses include actions to prevent spread (personal and public-health aspects) and to reduce misconceptions and social harm (quote 4). Therefore the infectious nature directly motivates strategies addressing both personal symptom management and social/ transmission-related consequences, making this option correct.

48.Option: The availability of national public health programs, which enables individuals to access specialized treatment and develop confidence in managing their condition
Evidence: The Comprehensive Measures for HTLV-1 was endorsed by the Japanese government in 2010 and the medical system in Japan is relatively well developed [25].

In Japan, the public initiatives of Comprehensive Measures for HTLV-1 include infection-prevention measures, such as the inclusion of HTLV-1 antibody testing in antenatal pregnancy screening, and measures to increase awareness and provide information, such as the website of the Ministry of Health, Labor for providing information on HTLV-1 infection and associated diseases, and published materials to increase public awareness [26].
Although measures at the national and municipal levels are being expanded, the concerns and hardships for individuals with HAM/TSP remain endless.
Participants understood that accessing care from HAM/TSP specialists is difficult, to the extent that even diagnosis of HAM/TSP can be time-consuming.
48.Rationale: The passage notes that national programs and public initiatives exist (quotes 1–2), which can support prevention and awareness activities. However it also emphasizes that despite these measures, patients continue to experience persistent concerns and hardships and that access to specialists can be difficult (quotes 3–4). The question asks for the factor most likely to influence development of self-management strategies addressing both personal and social consequences; the passage places greater emphasis on lack of awareness and infectiousness as drivers. Thus availability of programs is not presented as the primary influence on development of these combined strategies and is therefore incorrect.

49.Option: The persistence of elevated serotonin levels and the resulting downstream physiological responses, such as growth promotion, which may counteract intended therapeutic effects
Evidence: Parasitic flatworms have also been shown to actively transport exogenous 5-HT from hosts across their tegument further suggesting functional importance for parasite survival within a host [16–18].

Exposure to 5-HT for 24 hours, in the absence of growth-enhancing media (RPMI), significantly increased the motility of F. hepatica newly excysted juveniles (NEJs) by over 130% at a concentration of 1 mM (Fig 5A).
Juvenile (4 week old) F. hepatica motility was further enhanced by over 230% when culture media (50% CS) was supplemented with 1 mM 5-HT and maintained for 28 days (S7 Fig).
juveniles maintained in a medium consisting of 50% chicken serum supplemented with 1 mM 5-HT over a 28-day period exhibited a statistically significant 33% increase in growth (Fig 6A and 6B).

Knockdown of FhTPH significantly reduced the motility of juvenile F. hepatica, consistent with an impaired ability to synthesize 5-HT endogenously. To validate that reduced motility could be functionally rescued by restoring serotonergic signaling, exogenous 5-HT was applied to FhTPH-silenced juveniles. Exposure to 1 mM 5-HT for 18 hours restored and enhanced motility of FhTPH-silenced juveniles by tenfold, confirming that the phenotype reflects impaired serotonin availability rather than irreversible dysfunction (Fig 5D).
the growth of juveniles increased significantly by 29.1% following RNAi-mediated knockdown of the 5-HT transporter gene (FhSERT) (Fig 6C).
49.Rationale: The passage demonstrates that exogenous/persistent serotonin taken up from the host strongly enhances motility and growth, and can rescue the phenotype caused by blocking endogenous synthesis (FhTPH knockdown). Therefore, if elevated serotonin persists in the host environment (or reuptake is impaired), it can overcome interventions and sustain parasite physiology. That persistence of extracellular 5-HT is thus a critical determinant of how durable a therapeutic effect (e.g., TPH inhibition or receptor blockade) will be over time.
